claims.text: A short-duration sub-critical anneal will improve the tensile ductility of as-processed HfZrTiTa0.53.
A short-duration sub-critical anneal will improve the uniform tensile elongation of HfZrTiTa0.53.
The anneal will not significantly degrade the alloy's yield or compressive strength.
The anneal will not significantly degrade impact-triggered energy release.
As-produced HfZrTiTa0.53 has a yield strength of approximately 786 MPa.
As-produced HfZrTiTa0.53 has a compressive strength of approximately 1314 MPa.
The 13.5% terminal strain reported for HfZrTiTa0.53 is a tensile-ductility baseline.
Sub-critical annealing will produce a modest bimodal grain-size distribution.
Sub-critical annealing will reduce dislocation density at grain boundaries.
Sub-critical annealing will produce a more nearly equilibrium grain-boundary structure.
Sub-critical annealing will relieve residual stresses in HfZrTiTa0.53.
Sub-critical annealing will cause limited grain coarsening.
Sub-critical annealing will promote recovery of dislocation structures.
Residual-stress relief and dislocation recovery will enhance dislocation mobility during tensile loading.
The anneal-induced microstructure will delay tensile strain localization.
Uniform tensile elongation will increase by approximately 20–30% relative to the stated 13.5% baseline.
Yield and compressive strengths will remain within approximately 10–15% of their original values after annealing.
Impact-triggered energy release will show little to no change after annealing.
As-processed HfZrTiTa0.53 has demonstrated high energy release during impact tests.
Prior reports support the potential of controlled annealing to improve ductility without substantial loss of strength or energy release.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis alternately treats 13.5% as terminal strain, terminal tensile strain, and the baseline for uniform elongation. Terminal strain and uniform tensile elongation are distinct measurements, so the quantitative comparison is internally mismatched.
